intro-ecosystems-s1.title: Two warblers in one spruce forest
intro-ecosystems-s1.html:
A field biologist spent three summers watching two warbler species that eat the same kind of caterpillar in the same spruce forest. She expected one species to push the other out. Instead, both stayed common. Species A fed almost entirely in the top third of the trees, while species B fed on the lower branches near the trunk. In a stand where storms had snapped off the treetops, species A was rare and species B was common. She concluded that the two species can share the forest because each uses a different part of it.

Invented passage for practice.

nitrogen-cycle-s2.title: Beans in the rotation
nitrogen-cycle-s2.html:
A farmer who grows corn year after year adds nitrogen fertilizer every spring. A neighbor plants soybeans every other year instead of corn. The neighbor says the soybeans "put nitrogen back in the ground for free," so the corn that follows needs less fertilizer. Soybeans are legumes; their roots carry swellings, called nodules, that house bacteria. The neighbor adds that less fertilizer also means less nitrate washing into the creek.

trophic-levels-s1.title: Wolves return to a valley
trophic-levels-s1.html:
After wolves were brought back to a mountain valley, park staff noticed changes beyond the wolves themselves. Elk, the wolves’ main prey, became fewer and spent less time browsing in open riverbanks, where they were easy to catch. Willow shrubs along the river, which elk had been eating down to stubs, grew taller. A ranger argues that the wolves helped the willows, even though wolves never eat plants. A visiting scientist cautions that a run of wetter years also helped the willows grow, so the wolves may deserve only part of the credit.

Invented passage for practice, loosely based on reports from western North America.

food-webs-s2.title: Sea otters and kelp forests
food-webs-s2.html:
Along parts of the North Pacific coast, sea otters were hunted almost to extinction for their fur in the 1700s and 1800s. Where otters disappeared, sea urchins, which graze on kelp, became very numerous, and many kelp forests were reduced to bare rock called "urchin barrens." Where otters were protected and returned, urchins became scarce and kelp grew back, along with the many fish that shelter in kelp. Ecologists use this as an example of how one predator can shape a whole community, though they note that storms, water temperature and urchin disease also affect kelp.

Invented passage for practice, summarizing widely reported ecology of North Pacific kelp forests.
